questions.question: What is panel data (or longitudinal data), and what makes it unique?
questions.solution_html:
• Panel data
  • • Definition: the same cross-sectional units (individuals, firms, countries) observed over
  • several time periods
  • • Uniqueness: it combines cross-section and time-series dimensions, which controls for
  • unobserved heterogeneity, gives more variation, less collinearity and more degrees of
  • freedom, and allows dynamic analysis.
  • Normality of the errors (for inference)
questions.final_answer: Normality of the errors (for inference)
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: What is heteroscedasticity in an econometric model?
questions.solution_html:
• Heteroscedasticity
  • • Variance of the error term is not constant across observations: Var(uᵢ) = σᵢ²
  • • Example, such as consumption variance rising with income
  • • Consequence: OLS is unbiased but inefficient, and standard errors are biased
questions.final_answer: • Consequence: OLS is unbiased but inefficient, and standard errors are biased

  • • Narrower confidence intervals and larger t-values

questions.question: "Independent variables should be truly independent in a multiple regression / model." Examine the statement.
questions.solution_html:
• "Independent variables should be truly independent"
  • • Strictly, the regressors must not be perfectly linearly related (no perfect multicollinearity)
  • • Some correlation among regressors is acceptable, but high correlation inflates standard
  • errors and makes estimates unstable
  • • What is essential is that regressors are uncorrelated with the error term (exogeneity). So
  • the statement is only partly correct
questions.final_answer: the statement is only partly correct
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain how dummy variables are used to represent qualitative / characteristics such as gender, religion, and marital status in an econometric model.
questions.solution_html:
• Dummy variables
  • • Meaning: binary (0/1) variables that quantify qualitative attributes
  • • Gender example: Yᵢ = α + βDᵢ + uᵢ, with D = 1 for male and 0 for female. α is the
  • mean for the base category and β is the differential effect
  • • Religion and marital status
  • • For m categories use (m − 1) dummies, with one category as the base. Using m
  • dummies causes the dummy variable trap, i.e., perfect multicollinearity
  • • Interpretation of coefficients relative to the base category
  • • Mention of interaction (slope) dummies, or a worked example of a multi-category case
questions.final_answer: • Mention of interaction (slope) dummies, or a worked example of a multi-category case
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Illustrate how simple linear regression is utilized in empirical economics by / formulating four distinct models grounded in economic theory.
questions.solution_html:
• Four simple regression models
  • Any four models, with equation, variable definitions and expected sign, at 1.5 each
  • • Keynesian consumption function: C = β + β Y + u, (0 < β₁ < 1)
  • $ #

questions.question: Explain how multicollinearity affects standard errors and t-values.
questions.solution_html:
• Multicollinearity, standard errors and t-values
  • • Meaning of multicollinearity: high correlation among regressors
  • • Effect on standard errors: Var(β=ⱼ) = σ² = (σ²/Σxⱼ²) × VIF. As Rⱼ²
  • approaches 1, variance and standard error become very large, and confidence intervals
  • widen
  • • Effect on t-values: since t = β=ⱼ / se(β=ⱼ), inflated standard errors give small, insignificant
  • t-values even when R² is high and the F-test is significant. This leads to Type II errors
  • and unstable estimates
questions.final_answer: and unstable estimates
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the concepts of sampling distribution, point estimation, and interval / estimation in linear regression. Discuss the role of standard error in estimating regression coefficients.
questions.solution_html:
• Sampling distribution, point and interval estimation
  • • Sampling distribution: the probability distribution of an estimator over repeated samples
  • e.g., β=₁ ~ N(β₁,σ²/Σxᵢ²)
  • • Point estimation: a single sample value (β=₀,β=₁) used to estimate the parameter
  • • Interval estimation: β= ± t(α/2,n−2)·se(β=), a range with a stated confidence level
  • • Role of the standard error: se(β=₁) = σ̂/√Σxᵢ² measures precision, determines the width
  • of the interval and is used in t-tests
questions.final_answer: of the interval and is used in t-tests
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the importance of the critical region in making a decision about the / null hypothesis.
questions.solution_html:
• Importance of the critical region
  • • Definition: the set of test-statistic values for which H₀ is rejected
  • • Its size equals the significance level α, the probability of a Type I error
  • • Decision rule: reject H₀ if the statistic falls in the critical region, otherwise do not reject
  • • One-tailed versus two-tailed regions, with critical values
  • • Importance: it gives an objective rule, controls the Type I error rate and affects the power
  • of the test
  • • A diagram of the normal or t distribution earns the marks for the relevant point.
questions.final_answer: • A diagram of the normal or t distribution earns the marks for the relevant point
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: How is R2 calculated using ESS and TSS?
questions.solution_html:
• R² using ESS and TSS
  • • Definitions: TSS = Σ(Yᵢ − Ȳ)²,ESS = Σ(Ŷᵢ − Ȳ)²,RSS = Σûᵢ²
  • • Decomposition: TSS = ESS + RSS
  • • Formula: R² = ESS/TSS = 1 − RSS/TSS
  • • Interpretation: lies between 0 and 1, and measures the proportion of variation in Y
  • explained by the model. A higher value means a better fit
questions.final_answer: explained by the model. A higher value means a better fit

questions.question: Explain how multicollinearity affects standard errors and t-values.
questions.solution_html:
• Multicollinearity, standard errors and t-values

  • • Effect on standard errors: Var(β=ⱼ) = σ² = (σ²/Σxⱼ²) × VIF. As Rⱼ²
  • approaches 1, variance and standard error become very large, and confidence intervals
  • widen
  • • Effect on t-values: since t = β=ⱼ / se(β=ⱼ), inflated standard errors give small, insignificant
  • t-values even when R² is high and the F-test is significant. This leads to Type II errors
  • and unstable estimates

questions.question: Explain the importance of the critical region in making a decision about the / null hypothesis.
questions.solution_html:
• Importance of the critical region
  • • Definition: the set of test-statistic values for which H₀ is rejected
  • • Its size equals the significance level α, the probability of a Type I error
  • • Decision rule: reject H₀ if the statistic falls in the critical region, otherwise do not reject
  • • One-tailed versus two-tailed regions, with critical values
  • • Importance: it gives an objective rule, controls the Type I error rate and affects the power
  • of the test

questions.question: How is R2 calculated using ESS and TSS?

  • • Formula: R² = ESS/TSS = 1 − RSS/TSS
